BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: However, Wednesday evening, a closed Pacific low pressure system brings a more prolonged precipitation event. Precipitation with this system is most likely Wednesday evening through Thursday morning on the eastern side of the low.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Cool and dry conditions expected tonight through Sunday morning with patchy valley fog in the mountains.
- Light valley rain and mountain snow tomorrow evening in southeast Oregon, moving into southwest Idaho by Monday morning.
- Cooler and unsettled pattern continuing next week with snow levels potentially lowering to valley floors by the end of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The cold front has shifted to eastern Idaho this afternoon, with some lingering stratus cloud cover over the West Central/Boise Mountains. Trinity Mountain SNOTEL reported 7 inches of snow with this frontal passage and rainfall totals in the Snake River Valley ranged from 0.10-0.50 inches. Cool, dry, and breezy conditions will continue through most of the day on Sunday, with patchy fog tomorrow morning in higher elevation valleys. Another line of valley rain showers and mountain snow will move into southeast Oregon by midday on Sunday. Rainfall accumulations will range from 0.05-0.15 inches of rain with only a few inches of snow at higher peaks. This line will then gradually move into southwest Idaho overnight Sunday into Monday. Snow levels will stay between 5500-6500 feet MSL through Sunday and during the day on Monday, dropping off to 4500-5500 by Monday night. This will bring minor snow accumulations on Highway 55 and 21 on Monday night. Temperatures will linger a few degrees above normal today and tomorrow, still about ten degrees cooler than it has been this week.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Weather in the long term is seasonally typical in terms of temperature, but with continual moisture supporting rounds of precipitation through next week. Tuesday, temperatures finally cool to near normal as a weakening longwave trough moves through the region. Down from 5-10 degrees above normal the day before, cooler air settles in for the week and drops snow levels to around 4-5 kft MSL. These higher snow levels will support a couple inches of snow in mountains and mountain valleys. In lower elevations, up to 0.2 inches of rainfall are possible. Precipitation heads east and the seasonal temperatures and cooler air mass move in. There is a very low chance of snow in lower elevations with this system, as snow levels aren't projected to fall to valley floors until Wednesday morning; well after precipitation has ended. Conditions briefly dry out Wednesday as a ridge warms up the cold morning temps back to normal that afternoon.

However, Wednesday evening, a closed Pacific low pressure system brings a more prolonged precipitation event. Precipitation with this system is most likely Wednesday evening through Thursday morning on the eastern side of the low. Guidance suggests the core of the low will track south of the forecast area, meaning as the peak moisture leaves the area, lingering wraparound moisture will continue precipitation through at least Friday morning with isolated coverage through Saturday morning. Again, snow levels around 4-5 kft MSL will support a couple inches of snow on smaller mountains and in mountain valleys. But, on the highest ridges and summits 6 to 10 inches of snow become possible as snow ratios rise in colder temperatures and orographic lift increases precipitation efficiency. Again, up to 0.2 inches of rainfall are possible in lower elevations. The colder air behind the closed low only drops temperatures by a few degrees, but enough for snow levels to approach valley floors by Saturday morning. With a 10% chance of precipitation in trailing showers there is again a low chance for valley snow. A ridge will begin to build between the exiting low and a strengthening closed low off the Pacific NW coast through the rest of the weekend.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: That shortwave will quickly move off to the northeast as an upper low moves onto the West Coast. The progression of this upper low/trough Thursday into the weekend is highly uncertain.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Scattered rain and mountain snow showers today.
- Areas of fog are expected again Sunday morning, including the northern I-25 corridor and I-70 corridor.
- A return to mild and dry conditions Sunday through Tuesday.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Fog has begun to develop over parts of the east Colorado plains. Current webcams and observations show visibilities deteriorating over much of Lincoln County and parts of Elbert County, particularly along I-70. We have opted to issue a Dense Fog Advisory for Lincoln County at this time, but it may need to be expanded to surrounding counties as the fog continues to spread in the overnight hours. Visibilities may drop to less than 1/4 mile at times, and this has already been observed in Limon over the last hour. We expect visibilities to improve by late Sunday morning. We have adjusted low temperatures over the eastern Colorado plains tonight to better reflect the heat-trapping effect of the fog and low clouds.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A negatively tilted trough is moving over the area this afternoon. Moisture has increased significantly at mid and upper levels as this system approached the area. As of early this afternoon, the DCVZ was just to the east of Denver, with very light showers to its east and north. We still have a bit of a dry layer around 750mb across the plains, and with how light the precip is, it could struggle to make it to the ground in some areas until the layer starts to saturate more. Overall rain amounts are expected to be very light for much of the plains. Snow showers are moving into the mountains from the west and south as of early this afternoon. Coverage of snow showers this afternoon and evening will be best south of I-70, with most likely accumulations around a trace to 3 inches above 9000ft. Elevations around 8000ft to 9000ft could see a rain/snow mix today, but accumulations are unlikely.

Overnight, we're expecting more fog development across the plains. The REFS currently has a medium to high chance (50-75%) that portions of the I-70 and northern I-25 corridors will see fog with visiblities less than 0.5 mile in the early morning. Fog should start to clear around 10AM give or take an hour.

Upper level ridging begins to build over the area again on Sunday. Warmer and drier conditions will prevail Sunday through much of Tuesday. On Tuesday, an upper level trough will move onto the West Coast. Winds at mid levels will strengthen as the pressure gradient tightens between the upper ridge and trough. However, the strongest winds are forecast to remain to the south and east of our area. The trough will weaken and move east, sending a shortwave through the area early Wednesday. Precip chances will increase late Tuesday in the higher terrain as the shortwave approaches. The shortwave will be moving rather quickly and the southwesterly to westerly winds aloft are not super favorable for our area, so impacts from this event will be rather limited with snow totals around an inch or less for the higher elevations. For the plains, a cold front is forecast to move through sometime Wednesday, bringing slightly cooler temps for Wednesday into the end of the work week. Rain chances remain low (<20%) for the plains with the this system.

That shortwave will quickly move off to the northeast as an upper low moves onto the West Coast. The progression of this upper low/trough Thursday into the weekend is highly uncertain. A couple of days ago, models had a slower moving closed low headed towards the four corners region, now the most recent runs have a quicker moving more open wave going over and out of the area by late Saturday. The former is much more favorable for snowfall across our area, which is why we've seen a steady downward trend in precip amounts in the ensemble members. However, we are still quite a ways out, so things could swing back the other direction. We'll be keeping a close eye on this system.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Seasonal temperatures will stick around on Thursday with little to no weather impacts expected. Some lingering breezy conditions are still likely west of the Laramie Range on Thursday, but the rest of the forecast area will see a quiet day.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dense fog is possible again overnight tonight into Sunday morning, with a chance for a few showers along and south of the I-80 corridor.
- A slightly more active pattern is expected into the middle of next week, with low precipitation chances returning Wednesday into Thursday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A gloomy rest of the day is in store for us, as SE upslope flow is in place along and east of the I-25 corridor. This has resulted in rather widespread fog and low clouds throughout this morning, with some gradual clearing being observed via visible satellite imagery especially across portions of Laramie and Platte Counties in SE Wyoming. Low clouds and fog looks to linger in some areas of the NE Panhandle mainly south of the Pine Ridge, with a handful of locations currently observing visibilities between 1/2 to 1 mile. Overall expecting a gradual, but slight lifting of cloud bases from west to east throughout the afternoon, however most locations will still be impacted by at least some low cloud cover before the onset of more fog development after sunset into the overnight period. As many locations across the Nebraska Panhandle are still underneath a thick layer of low clouds, decreased high temperatures by around 5 degrees, with most locations east of the I-25 corridor struggling to get out of the 40s (which is actually normal for this time of year!).

A weak shortwave trough will continue to dig south and east of our area this evening and overnight, with the bulk of the forcing for ascent remaining well to our south in portions of Colorado. Overall, kept PoPs low (15-20%) for portions along and south of the I-80 corridor where some showers may manage to creep into our area from the south, though these are expected to be quite spotty and shouldn't amount to much in the way of beneficial moisture. One exception will be over the higher terrain of the Sierra Madre and Snowy Ranges, where there are currently some weak (<25 dBZ) radar returns, though not confident that much is making it to surface as mesonet observations are reporting 15-20 degree surface dewpoint depressions and WYDOT cameras aren't showing anything evident. Kept the highest PoPs (40-50%) over these higher elevations before 06Z as the system gradually move out of our area, but don't think anything will amount to much more than 1-2 inches of snow (if anything) on the mountain peaks.

For the lower elevations east of the Laramie Range, fog and poor visibilities will be the main hazard overnight under the upslope flow regime. Not confident in how widespread or dense the fog will be, but can anticipate a similar pattern to last night into early this morning which warranted a Dense Fog Advisory for much of the Nebraska Panhandle along with portions of Platte and Goshen Counties. Unlike today, expecting a faster dissipation of fog and low clouds tomorrow morning as 500 mb height rises and ridging builds in across much of the Central United States. As a result, tomorrow should be 5-10 degrees warmer than today, peaking in the mid to upper 50s east of the I-25 corridor, with slightly cooler upper 40s to low 50s to the west. Similar to the past couple of days, may need to bump forecast highs down a bit in areas where low clouds manage to hang on a bit longer.

Can expect further warming heading into the beginning of the work week as the ridge continues to amplify to our east, placing us in SW flow aloft. Dry conditions will persist through Monday, with highs potentially reaching the low to mid 60s east of the Laramie Range.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The majority of the long term will feature relatively benign weather with a return to more seasonable temperatures and breezy conditions. Picking up on Tuesday, this will likely be the last day of above average temperatures as the ridge continues to push eastward away from the CWA. High temperatures will be in the 50s and 60s which is still anywhere from 10 to 15 degrees above average for mid-November.

A pattern change will arrive on Wednesday as a trough swings into the Rockies. A cold front will move across the area, late Tuesday night or early Wednesday morning, leading to high temperatures in the 40s and 50s--roughly average for this time of year. This front will be mostly dry, with predominately west winds promoting a dry downslope environment. The mountains, however, could see a quick shot of snow, with the Sierra Madre Range picking up a few inches of accumulation. The Snowys will likely be shadowed and not see much in the way of accumulations. The bigger concern with the frontal passage will be strong winds. Marginal high winds will be possible as MSLP gradients compress from the front. Winds aloft will increase up to about 50 kts with decent subsidence, so cannot rule out 60 MPH gusts during the day in the typical southeast Wyoming wind prones.

Seasonal temperatures will stick around on Thursday with little to no weather impacts expected. Some lingering breezy conditions are still likely west of the Laramie Range on Thursday, but the rest of the forecast area will see a quiet day. Friday into the weekend, things could get interesting with a potential impactful winter storm. Of course, its still over a week away with plenty of time for models to come to a solution, but there is a chance for accumulating snow and windy conditions.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: The models continue to advertise another storm Friday and Saturday although the trends are shifting towards an open wave, much like the previous two systems.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread valley rain and mountain snow showers are expected through the evening. Travel could be impacted by snow covered roads.
- Quiet conditions return Sunday afternoon and Monday before another round of precipitation on Tuesday and Wednesday.
- There is another potential system on Friday and Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A shortwave trough is currently tracking over the area. It has resulted in widespread rain and snow showers. Snow levels made it down to about 7 kft this morning and those may slightly rise through out the day, especially if there is a break in the precipitation. The southern mountains are still favored to receive an additional 1-4" of snow with lesser amounts for the central and northern mountains. Rain amounts have reached 0.50" in spots with another 0.25" possible. Showers will start to dissipate this evening with most places dry by midnight. Tomorrow and Monday look to be mostly dry with slightly warmer temperatures.

Another shortwave trough very similar to the current is expected to impact the area on Tuesday and Wednesday. We should expect similar precipitation amounts and snow levels (7-9 kft). This system is slightly cooler, but the bulk of the precipitation is ahead and along the front. When the cold front arrives on Wednesday most of the showers will be decreasing in coverage. Snowfall amounts are much like the current system with the highest totals in southern mountains around 4-8" and lesser amounts further north.

The models continue to advertise another storm Friday and Saturday although the trends are shifting towards an open wave, much like the previous two systems. Due to the model inconsistency confidence is not high at this point, but with an open wave the precipitation amounts have trended downward. Timing will be something to watch with this wave as it may bring the snow levels down to some of the valleys Friday night into Saturday morning. Although once again the bulk of the precipitation is forecasted to occur ahead of the coldest air, so it does not appear the valleys will get much attm.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Thursday Through Saturday...A dry cold front dropping south across the eastern plains late Wed night will drop temps a few degrees across the plains on Thu, otherwise conditions remain dry until late Thu night when the next system starts to move into western CO.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Upper system crosses the region tonight, bringing snow to the mountains and showers to the high valleys and eastern plains mainly this evening.
- Areas of fog for the San Luis Valley and portions of the plains overnight tonight.
- Another mountain snow event late Tuesday into Wednesday.
- Unsettled weather continues into the next weekend, with another system crossing the Rockies starting Friday.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Have ended the Winter Weather Advisory for the San Juans, as area web cams show clearing skies and only a few lingering flurries.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...Upper system is pushing east across CO this afternoon, producing extensive cloud cover and widespread showers to much of the forecast area, as well as snow to the higher terrain, especially the Continental Divide as well as Pikes Peak.Temps as of 1 PM have warmed into the 40s for the high valleys, and 40s to around 50F for much of the eastern plains.

Tonight...Upper low is forecast to continue sliding east-southeast across the region this evening, strengthening as it starts to close off over the OK and TX Panhandles tonight. A few thunderstorms are possible this afternoon and early evening as colder air advects in from the north, all the while activity will start to diminish from west to east through the night. The ongoing Winter Weather Advisory for the eastern San Juan Mts expires at 9 PM which seems reasonable. Shower and storm activity for the eastern mts and plains will drop off considerably by midnight with lingering activity across the far eastern plains through the overnight hours. As cooler air moves in and cloud cover starts to thin, areas of fog are probable for the San Luis Valley and portions of the plains overnight tonight through Sunday morning, and have included that mention in the grids. Previously there was some concern of frozen precip over Monument Hill and northern El Paso County tonight, and though that still may occur in spots, this system is moving quick enough that there is less concern now. Will continue to monitor that through the night. Overnight lows tonight will be in the 20s for the high valleys, and 30s for the plains.

Sunday and Sunday night...A cool but essentially dry day on tap for the region tomorrow as the upper low slowly moves east, and a temporary ridge of high pressure moves across the Great Basin and Rocky Mts. Patchy fog will likely linger through the morning, and cloud cover will last the longest across the far eastern plains near the eastern border, so the mts and high valleys will see more sun and slightly warmer afternoon highs. Look for highs in the upper 40s to mid 50s for the high valleys, while the plains remain in the mid 40s to right around 50F.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Monday...Dry and warmer as a temporary upper ridge over the region gradually pushes east, with the ridge axis pushing east through the afternoon as the next feature approaches from the west. Plan on high temps in the 50s for the high valleys, and 50s to around 60F for the plains.

Tuesday and Wednesday...Models are still in agreement on another quick-moving system crossing the region mid-week as an open wave, bringing another shot of snow to the higher terrain late Tuesday through Wednesday. Wind-driven snow will occur along the Continental Divide, with advisory snow amounts likely for the eastern San Juan Mts. Across the eastern plains, strong southwest flow and lee troughing will help boost temps well into the 60s. High temps across the plains both days will be in the upper 50s to mid 60s, while the high valleys will warm into the upper 40s to mid 50s on Tue, then just the 40s on Wed.

Thursday Through Saturday...A dry cold front dropping south across the eastern plains late Wed night will drop temps a few degrees across the plains on Thu, otherwise conditions remain dry until late Thu night when the next system starts to move into western CO. Beyond that, forecast confidence drops off. There remains a lot of questions concerning the next weather feature for the region beginning Friday, with long range models in disagreement on how this will pan out. Models do indicate another system pushing across the region late Thu night through Sat, but whether this will be another quick hit or something more substantial remains a mystery. Key phrase for now will be unsettled. Moore

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: The Thursday/Friday storm continues to have little run-to-run consistency. ~60% of ensemble members bring a closed low through the area while the other 40% of members have a more progressive open wave.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Guidance is trending slightly warmer with the upcoming two storms on Tuesday/Wednesday and Thursday/Friday which will limit the valley snow potential.
- There is still a high amount of uncertainty regarding the late week storm.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A cold front has moved through the CWA with lingering mountain snow remaining across areas that do well in northwest flow. This period of northwest flow hasn't been as efficient as some of the guidance suggested yesterday so only another inch or two of snow is expected across the terrain before drier air starts to move into the region.

Ridging will quickly build into the area later tonight and persist through Sunday and Monday. The coldest temperatures of the season will develop overnight tonight with most locations, outside of lower Washington county getting near or below freezing. High temperatures will warm back up 3-8 degrees above normal Sunday and Monday before another negatively tilted trough moves in for Tuesday.

The 700 mb temperatures associated with the trough on Tuesday have trended slightly warmer in the most recent guidance. This will limit the valley snow probabilities with current snow levels getting down to 5500-6000 feet by Wednesday morning before conditions start to dry. This trough looks very similar to the one that moved through today. It will be a fast moving trough with a cold front that will bring widespread valley rain and mountain snow to the entire CWA with the highest totals favored across the southern mountains. Snow amounts will be between 3-8 inches with 5-10 inches across the southern mountains.

The Thursday/Friday storm continues to have little run-to-run consistency. ~60% of ensemble members bring a closed low through the area while the other 40% of members have a more progressive open wave. This system has also trended slightly warmer over the last several model runs which will decrease the potential for valley snowfall.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: You could trigger an avalanche where you find more than 10 inches of new, dense snow forming a slab over weak snow on steep, shady slopes above treeline.

Watch for cracking or collapsing in the new snow, as these are clear warning signs that a slab has formed. Safer travel conditions can be found on lower-angled slopes and at lower elevations where less new snow fell.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: A few inches of new snow late on Saturday won't be enough to raise avalanche concerns. Most slopes don't have enough snow for avalanches and are safe for travel. At high elevations, steer around isolated spots of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has yet to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. Except on the steepest, highest-elevation, north-facing slopes, the mountains are snow-free. Avalanches will be unlikely until a deeper, layered snowpack builds. Once winter does arrive, even a small amount of snow with enough wind can create unstable avalanche conditions. If you're traveling in the mountains during or after a storm, be wary of steep, wind-loaded features at upper elevations and watch out for terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information as more snow accumulates
hazard_discussion: Due to a warm and dry fall season, the mountains in our forecast zones remain mostly dry, with little to no snow on the ground. As you're waiting for winter to arrive and the mountain snowpack to stack up, here are a few things to consider:
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. If you are at high elevations and observe more than about 6 inches of new or wind-drifted snow, or see shooting cracks, steer around steep terrain features.
